70.2.1.1.text: Voyageurs carried two packs over this. Ninety pounds each. And sang. They'd have done this one twice before you finished your granola.
70.2.1.1.note: on Height of Land, Prairie, Curtain Falls, the Stairway, old-timer parties, Canadians

70.2.3.1.text: Nobody planted it in sixty years.

70.2.6.1.topic: head-high jack pine thicket, charred stumps, rock bared to the top. Old hands call it

70.2.6.2.text: the year it burned to Insula
70.2.6.2.topic: head-high jack pine thicket, charred stumps, rock bared to the top. Old hands call it

70.3.1.1.text: My dad's dad was underground at Soudan. I'm for anything that keeps the school open.

70.3.1.2.text: Thirty years in the woods. A paycheck's a paycheck.

70.3.1.3.text: My dad was underground at the Pioneer. He'd hate this one. It's not the mining, it's where.

70.3.1.4.text: My husband's for it. My sign's against. We have one mailbox. We manage.

70.3.2.1.text: Past the junction: the company's sign, lit, with a flower bed somebody keeps up.

70.3.2.2.text: Main Street. Canoe racks on half the cars, bait signs, a church supper on a sandwich board.

70.3.2.3.text: Mailboxes. A KETTLE — NO on a canoe rack, a KETTLE — YES on the next post.

70.3.2.4.text: The plant's lights, then three blue signs in a row, then a green one, then a blue.

70.3.2.5.text: Forty minutes of spruce. A logging truck, empty, going the other way.

70.3.2.6.text: Gravel and curves. A grouse in the road. No signs for twenty miles.

70.3.2.7.text: The old headframe on the ridge at Soudan. The lake to the left all the way.

70.3.2.8.text: A bar with motorboats on trailers out front. Not one sign about anything.

70.3.2.9.text: The '07 burn near the end of the Trail, jack pine head-high now, and lodges with their lights on.

70.3.2.10.text: Birch, gravel, a hand-painted board: CRAWLERS.

70.3.2.11.text: A long gravel road. A moose in the ditch, or a stump that looks like one.

70.3.2.12.text: Washboard. The truck rattles like it's telling you something.

70.3.2.13.text: A pickup behind you from town to the turnoff. Clean. It goes on past.
70.3.2.13.note: any road out of Ely, Only on a drive that starts at a store where    has happened, once a season.

70.3.2.14.text: A banner on the café: Northmark Open House, Farm Lake, Saturday. Free coffee.

70.3.2.15.text: Northmark's lot under the lights. Frank, in the grey shirt, at the office door with a man in a clean coat. The man is doing the talking.
70.3.2.15.note: 32-the-boys.md, Story override, 5.7:, Frank met, a drive through Ely between 21:00 and 05:00

70.3.2.16.text: A truck in the lot when you pull in. Engine running. Nobody gets out.
70.3.2.16.note: to the player's put-in, This is the tier-4 truck the bible puts in every lot, the card only names it.

70.3.2.17.text: Every gas station rack from Ely to Isabella has the Ledger on it this week.
70.3.2.17.note: the two weeks after the story breaks, through Ely

70.3.2.18.text: The company's sign at the junction. Still lit. The flower bed's been weeded.

70.3.2.19.text: Frank Kosir's yard: the sign's down. Just the two wire legs.

70.3.2.20.text: New survey stakes along the Little Gabbro road. Pink tape on every one.

70.3.2.21.text: A drill rig's noise, somewhere south, before you even open the door.

70.4.1.1.text: Half of Lake One's shore was cabins once. Then the government came round with a chequebook.

70.4.1.2.text: Before the bill the tow on Sag ran clear up the lake. After, we stopped at American Point where they told us. Still do.

70.4.1.3.text: The year they took the cans away, every Scout troop in Minnesota rewrote its menu at my counter.

70.4.1.4.text: The fire in '07 came up the lake in an afternoon. The blueberries were back the next August. I wasn't.

70.4.1.5.text: Did you know there was a railroad up here? Like a real one. I read it on a sign. Or a placemat.

70.4.1.6.text: I issued the first permits on this road by hand. Carbon paper. Nobody read them either.

70.4.1.7.text: My folks ran the resort when the road was gravel. Grandpa was underground at Soudan. Both of those are gone.

70.4.1.8.text: The spring the Pioneer shut, half my class moved to the Cities. I stayed and became a nurse. Somebody had to.

70.4.1.9.text: My family's been on both sides of that line a hundred years. The line's newer than we are.

70.4.1.10.text: The fall of Pagami we had smoke in the post office for a month. People mailed letters that smelled like a campfire.

70.4.1.11.text: They wanted to dam the whole border once. Before my time. I've measured what they'd have drowned.

70.4.1.12.text: The Fourth of July in '99 the sky went green over Poplar. My husband was on the roof. I've never let him forget it.

70.4.1.13.text: The winter the mill shut I made a tumpline. That's the whole story. It's a good tumpline.

70.4.1.14.text: Everybody up here has a year that's their year. I don't have one yet. I'm hoping for a nice one.

70.4.3.1.text: Leon wrote my dad up in '84 for a twenty-five horse on the wrong side of a line nobody could see. Dad was seventy-one. He paid it in ones, at the counter, counted out slow so Leon had to stand there.

70.4.3.2.text: Hal's father had a twenty-five on a ten-horse lake, half a mile past the sign. I wrote what I saw. I'd write it again. I also went to the funeral.

70.4.3.3.text: Ostrom shut a landing of mine in '97 for silt in a creek. He was right. I've never forgiven him for being right.

70.4.3.4.text: Norm's creek ran brown for eleven days. I have the readings. He sends me a card every Christmas anyway. It says 'Still brown.'

70.4.3.5.text: Ely people think the Boundary Waters is a suburb of Ely. We're very polite about it on the Trail.

70.4.3.6.text: The Trail people think they invented lake trout. Let them. They had to invent something.

70.4.3.7.text: Norm nailed his sign to the woodshed so the wind can't take it. Mine's on wire legs. Mine's fallen over twice. I put it back up both times. That's the difference between us.

70.4.3.8.text: Joanne patched my hand in '89 when I put a saw in it. Didn't charge me. I'd vote however she wanted on anything but this.

70.4.3.9.text: Myrna knows what everybody in Isabella got for Christmas since 1983. Never said a word. That's worse.

70.4.3.10.text: Thirty years at the post office, you learn what people send and you learn to forget it by suppertime.

70.4.3.11.text: They rent the dining room for the open house in August. Pay on time, tip the girls, put out free coffee, which annoys Deb, because it's her coffee.

70.4.3.12.text: Thirty years the Remote Area permit worked fine. Now you check in like it's an airport. Not my idea either.

70.4.3.13.text: Pete wants that plane on the Kek. Thirty years he's wanted it. He'll get there one of these summers and find out it's a plane.

70.4.3.14.text: That's Len in there. We were on the crews together. He was always friendlier than me.
70.4.3.14.note: That is all he says about Len until the arc gives more.

70.4.3.15.note: Brekke's day. She never says so.

70.4.3.16.text: We don't do the mine at the fire. That's the rule since 2016.

70.4.3.17.text: That's his rule. I just follow it because he's older.

70.4.3.18.text: I gave a statement in '77. They wrote down the half they wanted.

70.4.3.19.text: Aili Niemi doesn't come to church suppers since her brother's memorial. People signed the book she didn't know.

70.4.4.1.text: That pack's going to outlive both of us.

70.4.4.2.text: How'd the old tent do? Did it leak? It looks like it leaks.

70.4.4.3.text: Honestly? No idea. It was on the shelf when I started. Before my time. Ask the boss, but he'll say the same.

70.4.4.4.text: Did that old guy on the porch talk your ear off? He does that. He's nice, I think. He tipped me a dollar once for a coffee that cost a dollar.

70.4.4.5.text: Dan from the company was asking if you were around. I said you're always around. Was that okay? You are always around.

70.4.4.6.text: You get a lot of mail for somebody who doesn't live here. Kidding. You get none.

70.4.4.7.text: You look like you didn't sleep. Was it the loons? It's always the loons.

70.4.4.8.text: Somebody's parked in the lot every morning this week. Not a customer. I checked.

70.4.4.9.text: You're the canoeist in the paper. Everybody knows. I said 'what canoeist' to like nine people.

70.4.4.10.text: The boss says I'm not supposed to give you the good canoes anymore. I don't know why. I'm giving you a good one.

70.5.1.c1.text: Ever hear of a guide called Walt?

70.5.2.1.text: The guy who drowned? The kid at the outfitter said something. A few years ago, right?

70.5.2.2.text: No, sorry. We're from Iowa. We don't know anybody. We barely know each other.

70.5.2.3.text: Is he the one with the rock on the stump? Somebody said an old guide used to leave rocks.
70.5.2.3.note: Only at a starred site, with the stone in sight: the bible's day beat.

70.5.2.4.text: I think I read about that. Old guy, alone, October. My mom sent me the link and said 'see?'

70.5.2.5.text: Walt? Is he a ranger? We met a ranger. He was very nice. He asked about our food.

70.5.2.6.text: Oh, the paper thing! Are you the canoeist? You are, aren't you. Can I get a picture?

70.5.2.7.text: He wrote in rods? Who writes in rods. Oh. Everyone up here. Okay.

70.5.2.8.text: This is the most organised thing I've ever seen. My trip journal is just 'tired' and a drawing of a moose.

70.5.2.9.text: Is that a real lake? Can you look it up? We have no signal. Never mind.

70.5.2.10.text: That's beautiful handwriting. My grandpa wrote like that. He was an engineer. Everything was in capitals.

70.5.2.11.text: Babe, it's somebody's diary. Give it back.

70.5.3.1.text: Walt Haapala? Ely guide. Good with the clients. Didn't like the owners. Who does.

70.5.3.2.text: He'd go out alone in the fall. People thought it was strange. Fall's the best part. I thought it was sense.

70.5.3.3.text: They found his canoe on Birch. That was 2019. Sad business. He was seventy-something.

70.5.3.4.text: Knew him to wave to. He paddled like he was in no hurry and got there first.

70.5.3.5.text: His brother drowned too, way back. Bald Eagle, I want to say. Seventies. Same family twice. Imagine.
70.5.3.5.note: Old Ely hands only, never the name.

70.5.3.6.text: Walt? I don't talk about people who can't hear me.
70.5.3.6.note: A guarded one, that's the whole answer.

70.5.3.7.text: You've been asking a lot about Walt. Small town. People notice what you ask.

70.5.3.8.text: That's a guide's book. Wind first, always. Fish last. Feelings never.

70.5.3.9.text: NW 15, gusts 25. He knew what he was looking at.

70.5.3.10.text: Two cups out of habit. Huh.
70.5.3.10.note: Says nothing else. Hands it back.

70.5.3.11.text: My dad kept one of these. Forty years of them in a coffee can. Nobody's read them. Nobody's going to.

70.5.3.12.text: He went back and wrote on it later. Different pencil. People do that when they get old.

70.5.3.13.text: That's Walt's hand. I bought bait off him for six summers. He wrote the receipts like that.
70.5.3.13.note: Only keepers who knew him at a counter: Myrna, Ruth.

70.5.3.14.text: Lake One. Everybody's first night is Lake One. Guides called it that.

70.5.3.15.text: Kekekabic. Everybody says the Kek. You'd only spell it out on a permit.

70.5.3.16.text: Fourtown. Four Towns is what the old crowd on the Echo Trail say.

70.5.3.17.text: Little Saganaga. Long day out of Sawbill. Big lake trout.

70.5.3.18.text: That's his own name for it. Every guide has a few. Mine are worse.

70.5.3.19.text: the far end The far end of what? Every lake's got one.

70.5.4.1.text: Hundred and eighty-six rods, and he paced it himself. You can tell. Map says one-eighty-five.
70.5.4.1.when: The page has: A rod count

70.5.4.2.text: A question mark. My grandpa did that. Meant he wasn't going to tell anybody, including himself.
70.5.4.2.when: The page has: `?` alone on a line

70.5.4.3.text: Nobody all day. He liked that. Some people would hate that.

70.5.4.4.text: Everybody's got a camp somewhere. That's a cabin, to you.

70.5.4.5.text: Sparky, Whiskey, Teach. Sounds like a bunch.
70.5.4.5.when: The page has: The boys' nicknames
70.5.4.5.note: Nobody decodes them but the boys and Carol

70.5.4.6.text: June. That'll be his wife. Don't read that one to me.

70.5.4.7.text: V. Somebody he didn't want to write down.

70.5.5.3.text: So it's a treasure map for fish.

70.5.5.4.text: Why does he write so small?

70.5.5.5.text: He drew a fish! It's a bad fish.

70.5.5.6.text: Did he die? Mom, did he die?

70.5.5.7.text: A long time ago. He was very old.

70.5.5.9.text: Walt? Best walleye man between here and Insula. Never told a living soul a reef. I respected that and I hated it.
70.5.5.9.note: Old guides only. Soft, not a key: Insula is the Kitchen, which Hap and Tom decode anyway.

70.5.5.10.text: If that book has his spots in it, don't tell me. I'd never fish my own again.

70.5.5.11.text: Walt Haapala. Before me. They still talk about him at the district office. Mostly about his fire rings.

70.5.5.12.text: He camped legal. Mostly. Good for him.

70.5.5.13.text: We don't get your news over here. Who?

70.5.5.14.text: An American guide, alone, in October? We'd have heard if he came through. Unless he didn't want us to.
70.5.5.14.note: Only on the Quetico side, says nothing more.

70.5.5.15.text: Rods. You Americans and your rods. It's metres on this side. Well. It's rods on this side too.

70.5.5.16.text: That's his book. Put it away. We don't read a man's book. That's a rule older than the first-round rule.

70.5.5.17.text: Put that away. He'd come back from wherever he is to kill us.

70.5.5.18.text: Don't. I can't. Put it away.
70.5.5.18.note: Same refusal as the others, in his own voice. It is not one of his three tells and must not read as one: Bob and Frank refuse first, every time the three are together.

70.6.1.1.text: Old guide drowned on Birch a few years back. October. They found his canoe swamped. No paddle.
70.6.1.1.note: Moose Lake's reach and Ely side

70.6.1.2.text: The company's having its open house at Farm Lake in August. Free coffee and a slideshow. My brother-in-law goes for the coffee.

70.6.1.3.text: The state's supposed to decide on the Kettle thing this winter. They've been supposed to for a while.

70.6.1.4.text: A Finn kid drowned on Bald Eagle in the seventies. Ducks, they said. My dad was on the drag line.

70.6.1.5.text: Fella on the Stuart Portage at dusk, every Tuesday, no pack. Says 'evening' and keeps walking. Ollie, somebody said. Harmless.

70.6.1.6.text: There's a tabloid in Duluth paying for Sasquatch pictures again. Every summer. Somebody always takes the money.

70.6.1.7.text: The lights over Fourtown were out again last fall. Northern lights, mostly. Mostly.

70.6.1.8.text: Some grad student at the Moose River post wants to know where the wolves den. Good luck to her.

70.6.1.9.text: There's a plane in the Kek. Down by the north shore. On a calm day you can see the red.

70.6.1.10.text: Somebody found an old bootlegger's box up by Loon Lake once. Nothing in it but bottles.

70.6.1.11.text: There's lilacs on Basswood where an old fish camp was. June, they come out. Nobody planted them in sixty years.

70.6.1.12.text: Tom Becker's crew is going to haul that old sled off the lunch rock on Insula. People have opinions.

70.6.1.13.who: A retired local on a dock
70.6.1.13.text: Ice went out on the twenty-ninth. I write it down every year.

70.6.1.14.who: An old solo on a carry
70.6.1.14.text: Evening. Short one, this. Long one's next.

70.6.1.15.text: The decision's 'this winter' again. It's been this winter for three winters.

70.6.2.1.text: That pack's older than you. Canvas holds up. Just don't get it wet. Or do. It stays wet.

70.6.2.2.text: Is that vintage? That's so cool. Is it heavy? It looks heavy.

70.6.2.3.who: An old solo on a carry
70.6.2.3.text: You don't see those any more. My first one was like that. Tumpline and all.

70.6.2.4.text: That's a crew stencil, on the patch. Somebody's old work pack.

70.6.3.1.text: Tauno Kangas is talking to strangers on porches again. He doesn't do that.

70.6.3.2.text: Somebody's been asking about the old drill outfit at Farm. You don't hear that name much.
70.6.3.2.note: Any Ely-side keeper, after the player asked about Boreal at two places, this is tier 1's word

70.6.3.3.text: Walt's bunch go in out of Sawbill every August. Second week. Loud. They'll feed you.

70.6.3.4.text: BRM. That's Boreal. The old drill outfit. Seventies. Where'd you get that?
70.6.3.4.note: Region key B, any old Ely hand. Not before   .

70.6.3.5.text: Asking about Walt? Buy the man a coffee first. That's how it works up here.

70.6.4.1.text: Fella was asking which way you went. I said I don't know which way anybody goes. That's mostly true.
70.6.4.1.note: The keeper of the store where    or    happened, the next visit

70.6.4.2.text: Dan from the company's been at every counter this week. Shaking hands. He's good at it.

70.6.4.3.text: Party came off {lake}, said two fellas in a green Kevlar were asking after a solo. No rods.
70.6.4.3.note: Josie only, and only as the canary trap's echo (bible 5.7)

70.6.4.4.text: Two men in a green Kevlar camped across from us on {lastLake}. No fire, no rods. Waved like they practise it.
70.6.4.4.note: A party only, on that night

70.6.4.5.text: Fella bought three dozen leeches and left them on the step. Never seen that in thirty years.
70.6.4.5.note: The keeper where, never his name

70.6.4.6.text: There's another canoe behind us. Two guys. They're not in a hurry.

70.6.4.7.text: You're getting known. That's not always a compliment up here.

70.6.5.1.text: Somebody's camp got gone through on {lake}. Nothing taken. Folded everything. Who folds?
70.6.5.1.note: A party the schedule had within sight of the player's site on the day of, at their next fire or at a store

70.6.5.2.text: There's a woman in the Hog Creek bunkhouse says she's here to fish. Eleven days and one perch.
70.6.5.2.note: Hog Creek and its reach, from Maggie's arrival

70.6.5.3.text: The company's open house was busy this year. They had a map with colours on it. Everybody stood around it like it was a fish.

70.6.5.4.text: You look like somebody moved your stuff. You've got the face.

70.6.5.5.text: You're in it now, whatever it is. I'm not asking.

70.6.6.1.text: Somebody's canoe was loose on {lake} this morning. Paddle gone. They swam for it. In September.
70.6.6.1.note: A party near, or the keeper of the next store, never says it was the player's unless it was told by the player

70.6.6.2.text: There's a truck at {ep} every morning. Not a fisherman. Fishermen leave.
70.6.6.2.note: The keeper of the player's last put-in

70.6.6.3.text: Keep your canoe up the shore at night. Way up. I don't know why I said that.

70.6.6.4.text: Did you see the light on the point? Somebody's out without a fire.

70.6.7.1.text: Early start? You look like you paddled all night. Have a good one.
70.6.7.1.note: The dawn lot, the loading party only

70.6.8.1.text: Did you see the Ledger? Some canoeist found papers in the woods. The old drill outfit faked its water numbers. Nineteen seventy-six.
70.6.8.1.note: the two weeks after the story breaks

70.6.8.2.text: Carl Brekke's out at the company. 'Health reasons.' Sure.

70.6.8.3.text: The Forest Service is closing up that old trench by Bald Eagle. About time.

70.6.8.4.text: They're redoing the company's water work. Honest this time, they say. Tasha Strand's crew.
70.6.8.4.note: Farm, Bog, Hog Creek, next season

70.6.8.5.text: The sheriff opened the old file on the Bald Eagle kid and shut it again. Insufficient something.

70.6.8.6.text: The paper says the old guide didn't drown. Faked it. Went north. People are saying he's a hero. People are saying worse.
70.6.8.6.note: JN only, never more than what the story printed

70.6.8.7.text: Hey, are you the one from the paper? My dad says thank you. My uncle says something else.

70.6.8.9.text: Somebody sold the company some old papers. Maggie Tomczak wrote about it like it hurt.
70.6.8.9.note: the two weeks after her column

70.6.8.10.text: They got their permit. Drill rigs at Little Gabbro next spring.

70.6.8.11.text: Frank Kosir took his sign down. Twenty years he's had a sign. Wouldn't say why.

70.6.8.12.note: The bible's dropped tasks, said once, then the board just has none

70.6.8.13.text: Somebody said you're rich now? You don't look rich. No offence.

70.6.9.1.text: Walt used to put in at Lake One the first week the ice was off. Every year. You could set a clock.

70.6.9.2.text: Walt's bunch are in. Second week of August, like always. Three of them now.

70.6.9.3.text: October. Walt's month. Everybody's home but him.

70.6.9.4.text: Last trips. Skim ice in the bays by the twentieth. People who go out now know why they're going.

70.7.1.1.text: We came in at {fromEp} on Saturday. Last night was {lastLake}. Tonight's this.

70.7.1.2.text: We were wind-bound a day on {windLake}. Played cards. Someone lost a lot of M&Ms.

70.7.1.3.text: Best fish so far was a {catchSp}, {bestIn} inches. Don't ask who caught it. It wasn't him.

70.7.1.4.text: Saw {seen} this morning. Just stood there. We just stood there. Nobody did anything for a minute.

70.7.1.5.text: Tomorrow's {nextLake}. Is the carry bad? Don't tell me. Tell me after.

70.7.1.6.text: Sites were all taken on {lastLake} by four. We paddled till six. It was fine. It was not fine.

70.7.2.1.text: We have a spreadsheet. Day three has a column called 'feelings'. It's empty.

70.7.2.2.text: Somebody at the outfitter said 'a little breezy'. We are learning what that means.

70.7.2.3.text: We've been planning since January. Now we're here and nobody wants to leave the site.

70.7.2.4.text: There's signs all the way up from Ely. Yes, no, yes, no. Like a wedding where the families don't get along.

70.7.2.5.text: The guy who drowned? We heard. That's so sad. Alone, though. That's the part.

70.7.2.6.text: Did you see the paper? Somebody found the old company's stuff in the woods. With an old guide's tent. That's like a movie.

70.7.2.7.text: We found a square nail by the fire ring. Mom says it's history. I think it's a nail.
70.7.2.7.note: Only at a site near an old resort, or a cabin site

70.7.2.8.text: My dad brought me up when I was ten. Same lake. The site's smaller than I remember. Everything is.

70.7.2.9.text: There's rhubarb in the woods! Who planted rhubarb in the woods?

70.7.2.11.text: I think the outfitter said something about an old guide. I was counting children.

70.7.2.12.text: Nine of us and four canoes. That's the rule. The rule doesn't say they have to be quiet.

70.7.2.13.text: I took my first crew out of Moose Lake in '88. Walt Haapala was on the counter. He sold us a map and told us which half of it was wrong.
70.7.2.13.note: the guide is an old local by look

70.7.2.14.text: Is it true there's a Sasquatch? The guide says no but he says it like there is.

70.7.2.15.text: They're on the reef at dusk. That's all you get.

70.7.2.16.text: Thirty years we come up the same week. Same site, same reef, same argument about the reef.

70.7.2.17.text: Walt? He'd sit in his canoe on a reef and not fish. Just look at the water. You'd think he was praying. He was reading the bottom.

70.7.2.18.text: Day nine. I talked to a chipmunk for twenty minutes this morning. It had good points.

70.7.2.19.text: I come up alone because nobody else will get up at five. Turns out I don't either.

70.7.2.20.text: I passed him once on the Kek. He waved like he'd known me forty years. We'd never met. That was Walt, I found out later.

70.7.2.21.text: Somebody always leaves a white rock on that stump. Every time I come through, it's there. I leave it. Seems like a thing you leave.
70.7.2.21.note: At a starred site, the stone in sight, The bible's day beat

70.7.2.22.text: Where'd you come in? Good camp.

70.7.2.23.text: Food hung? Good. I have to ask. I ask the bears too.

70.7.2.24.text: There's a lot of old junk in the woods. Some of it's history. I'm supposed to know which.

70.7.2.25.text: We're hauling the sled off the lunch rock this month. Unless somebody gives me a reason.

70.7.2.26.text: We're closing up the old trench by Bald Eagle. Old damage. Nice to fix something on purpose.

70.7.2.27.text: You'll see more people on Basswood in an afternoon than we've seen all week.

70.7.2.28.text: Barbless? Barbless. Good. Leeches? I didn't see any leeches.

70.7.2.29.text: This was a mine town too, Atikokan. They closed around '80. We know how it goes. You still paddle.

70.7.3.1.text: Walt cooked. Now I cook. We've lost four pans to my cooking. We've lost no pans to Walt's.

70.7.3.2.text: First round's on you. That's Walt's rule. It's not my rule. I'd let you off.

70.7.3.3.text: Twenty-six trips with Walt. We missed '93. Somebody's daughter got married.

70.7.3.4.text: She's divorced now. Was it worth it?

70.7.3.5.text: You got enough to eat? Take this. Take two. We always bring too much.

70.7.3.6.text: If you're going out from here, I'll ring you a couple of spots. And a carry. You'll want the carry.

70.7.3.7.text: Four seventy-three rods both ways. We complain on the way in so we don't have to on the way out.

70.7.3.8.text: Sparky set the canoe on fire in '86. Not the whole canoe.
70.7.3.8.note: This exchange decodes Sparky. The bible (5.7) makes "the boys' stories at Little Sag" one of the two ways to learn it, so it belongs to the arc file's timing: it plays only when that file says the stories are told, and it then sets   . It is never in the random ambient pool.

70.7.3.9.text: It was a flare. It was mostly the flare.
70.7.3.9.note: This exchange decodes Sparky. The bible (5.7) makes "the boys' stories at Little Sag" one of the two ways to learn it, so it belongs to the arc file's timing: it plays only when that file says the stories are told, and it then sets   . It is never in the random ambient pool.

70.7.3.10.text: He'd go quiet on the last night. Sit on that rock. We let him be. We still let him be.
70.7.3.10.note: Last night, the 14th, before the reveal scene

70.8.1.1.text: That old thing? Came through the used lot, I'd guess. Every outfitter's back room has a bit of every other one's. Before my time, whoever had it.

70.8.1.2.text: Walt? He put in at Lake One every May, the first week the ice was off, when we were there. Bought one candy bar. Same kind every year. Never said what he was doing. Fishing, I supposed.

70.8.1.3.text: Polite. Paid cash. Looked at the lake a long time before he got in. Some people do that.

70.8.1.4.text: That's Lake One. The guides all called it that. Everybody's first night.
70.8.1.4.note: a nickname: the Front Porch, Ring Lake One

70.8.1.5.text: Tauno sits out there every morning since June. If he's talking to you, he likes you, or he's worried about you. Usually both.

70.8.1.6.text: Tauno, out front, mornings. Mary's in Tuesdays and Fridays. She typed for the old outfit, years ago.
70.8.1.6.note: asked where to ask, Ring nothing: both are here

70.8.1.7.text: Thursdays I keep the corner table for Len Saari and his friend from Duluth. Carl Brekke. Big tipper. Gold ring. I don't like him and I can't tell you why, which is the worst kind.

70.8.1.8.text: The company's open house is Saturday. In my dining room. Free coffee. Deb's furious. Come and eat a bar.

70.8.1.9.text: You've been back here more than anybody this summer. Sit. You look like you've been thinking.

70.8.1.10.text: Tauno said a name at the counter this morning. Out loud. In my café. I've never heard him say it. I gave him his coffee for nothing.

70.8.1.11.text: Tauno read the paper twice. Then he went and sat on the porch with nothing to look at. He looked happy. I think that's happy.

70.8.1.12.note: The warmest keeper, now plain, she never says why

70.8.2.1.text: Back room stuff came with the store. Some of it went to the lot, some of it came back. I don't ask whose. Used gear's used gear.

70.8.2.2.text: Before my time. Bought the place in '21. It came with a lot of canoes and a lot of opinions.
70.8.2.2.note: 31-guiding-years.md, 20-opening.md, His own line from    5.6, the bunkhouse question is   's

70.8.2.3.text: Never ran Moose. Ran Sag. Thirty years. Ask Nate where it lands, he drives it.

70.8.2.4.text: I was on Sag that fall. Heard it on the radio like everybody. Before my time here.
70.8.2.4.note: the drowning, Nothing about the wind or the search: that's Sheila's page

70.8.2.5.text: Marlys does Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Ran this counter twenty-some years. She knows where everything is, including what I've lost. Hap's on the porch weekends. Bring him a coffee, black.
70.8.2.5.note: asked where to ask, Ring nothing: both are here

70.8.2.6.text: Dan from the company. Nice kid. Coaches hockey. Asked if you rented here. I said everybody rents here.

70.8.2.7.text: Fella in a clean truck bought bait and didn't take it. Leeches on the step. I put them back in the tank. Waste not.

70.8.2.8.text: Somebody's in my lot at six every morning. Doesn't buy coffee. That's what gets me. Buy a coffee.

70.8.2.9.text: Marlys hung his picture. There, by the paddles. I'd have put it by the till. She's the boss of the wall.

70.8.3.1.text: Somebody's dad's. That's who owns all old gear. Somebody's dad.

70.8.3.2.text: Walt guided out of here for eight years. He cooked for his clients like they were his kids, and talked to them like they were his kids, too.

70.8.3.3.text: He was good. Then he wasn't here. Guides are like that. You look up and they're on the next road.

70.8.3.4.text: Tauno Kangas? No relation. Every third Finn up here is a Kangas. We share a phone book page.

70.8.3.5.text: Walt's bunch. The guys. They book Sawbill the morning the permits open. They've never once needed to. They're old and stubborn. Second week of August, they're in. Carol at the counter was married to one of them. Gene.
70.8.3.5.note: asked where to ask, Ring the Sawbill landing

70.8.3.6.text: The guys are in. They'll stop for leeches on the way and complain about the price. Every year. Same price.

70.8.3.7.text: A fella from the company came by with a card. I put it with the other cards. I have a drawer.

70.8.3.8.text: Denny was in here asking after you. He's sweet. He asks after everybody.
70.8.3.8.note: Denny's over-helping, seen from outside. Not a tell: he really does ask after everybody.

70.8.3.9.text: Bob came in with the paper folded to the page and didn't say anything. Just put it on the counter and bought leeches. That's Bob crying.

70.8.3.10.text: The guys said not to save them a spot for you. I'm just telling you what they said.

70.8.4.1.text: That's an Ely pack. You can tell by how much it weighs. They think weight builds character.

70.8.4.2.text: Ely guide. Came up the Trail twice that I know of. Once to look at the cliffs on Ottertrack. Once because he was lost, he said. He was never lost a day in his life.

70.8.4.3.text: Ottertrack has the clearest water up here. You can see your anchor on the bottom at twenty feet. He stood in his canoe and looked at it like it owed him something.

70.8.4.4.text: The Long Room. That's what the Ely guides called Ottertrack, the cliff stretch. I never called it anything. It's a lake.
70.8.4.4.note: the Long Room, if shown, Not a ring: Hap decodes it. Arvid confirms only that it's Ely talk.

70.8.4.5.text: There's a plane in the Kek. Nineteen-fifty, the winter before the planes stopped. The pilot swam out and walked to the resort. Pete Haldane wants it. Pete wants a lot of things.
70.8.4.5.note: the plane, while S5 is open

70.8.4.6.text: Nobody asks me anything. I'm at the end of the Trail. They'd need a reason.

70.8.4.7.text: The Ely papers came up the Trail a week late, like everything. Good story. Walt would've hated being in it.

70.8.4.8.text: Somebody sold something. Don't know who. Don't want to know. I'm at the end of the Trail.

70.8.5.1.text: Oh my gosh, it's so old. I love it. Is that canvas? You're so brave.

70.8.5.2.text: Before my time. Like way before. I think somebody said he was the guy who drowned on some lake by Ely? Sorry. I only know loons.

70.8.5.3.text: The Kek! I know that one. Kekekabic. I counted loons there. Eleven. Twelve if you count the one I think was a duck.
70.8.5.3.note: the Kek, if shown, Ring Kekekabic

70.8.5.4.text: A guy from the mining company left a card and a pen. The pen's nice.

70.8.5.5.text: Is it true you found, like, a mystery? That's the coolest thing that's ever happened to anyone I've rented a canoe to.

70.8.5.6.text: Somebody said you got paid a lot of money for something. Do you want to buy a loon print? They're forty dollars.

70.8.6.1.text: A Duluth pack, nineteen-seventies, canvas, leather straps replaced once. The patch is a crew patch. Whose, I couldn't say. I don't guess.

70.8.6.2.text: I wrote him up once. 1991. A fire ring the size of a hot tub on Nina Moose. I went back to measure it and he'd taken it down to one. The hot tub was somebody else's. I tore up the ticket. The only one in thirty-one years.

70.8.6.3.text: He camped legal. Mostly. He'd tell you which rules were his and which were yours.

70.8.6.4.text: October, alone, on the border. I read the summary. Two pages. I'd have written more. I always wrote more.

70.8.6.5.text: There's a man walks the Stuart Portage at dusk, Tuesdays and Thursdays. Ollie Pekkala. Rescue squad, forty years. Say 'evening'. That's how it starts with Ollie.
70.8.6.5.note: S1's thread, After, no ring: the portage is on the sheet

70.8.6.6.text: No one has asked me about you. I would tell you if they had. I keep a log.

70.8.6.7.text: I clipped the article. I clip everything. This one I read twice.

70.8.6.8.text: You'll want your permit at the counter before you go in. As always.

70.8.7.1.text: That's a crew patch, I'd guess. Somebody's old work pack. My dad had one like it for the mine. Smelled like the mine till the day he burned it.

70.8.7.2.text: I knew June. Walt's wife. June Mattila, from Tower. She taught my kid brother third grade. Too good for Walt, everybody said. Walt said it loudest.

70.8.7.3.text: She died in '08. He went out alone after. That's the order it went in. I don't know that one caused the other. People said so.

70.8.7.4.text: He didn't come to Vermilion much. Big water, motors. Not his kind of lake. He came once to bring June to see her mother's old place. They sat in the car a long time.

70.8.7.5.text: Dan Marolt was through. Gave me a hat. I'm wearing it. Doesn't mean anything. It's a good hat.

70.8.7.6.text: I'm for the mine. I've always been for the mine. I'm not for faking anything. Those are two different things and everybody's acting like they're one.

70.8.7.7.text: They got their permit. I should be happy. I'm wearing the hat. I'm happy.

70.8.8.1.text: Somebody loved that pack, hon. Look at the patches. You don't patch a thing you don't love.

70.8.8.2.text: I nursed his wife at the end. June. He brought a thermos every morning. Two cups. She couldn't drink hers by the last week. He poured it anyway.

70.8.8.3.text: Then for years he came to the home once a month to see Hap Johnsrud. Coffee and a bar. First Tuesday. And then he didn't. Hap asked after him for a year.

70.8.8.4.text: Hap's at Moose Lake weekends. His grandson drives him up. He'll talk your ear off and half of it'll be true and the other half will be better.
70.8.8.4.note: asked where to ask, Ring Moose Lake

70.8.8.5.text: Fourtown. The old crowd on this road call it Four Towns. My uncle did. Don't ask me why. Nobody knows.
70.8.8.5.note: Four Towns, if shown, Ring Fourtown

70.8.8.6.text: The paintings on North Hegman are older than anybody can say. Look from the canoe. Don't touch them.

70.8.8.7.text: A nice boy from the company left a card. I told him my sign's at the end of the drive and he said 'I saw.' He was very polite. I gave him a muffin.

70.8.8.8.text: I took the paper to Hap. He made me read it twice and then he said, 'He liked October.' That's all he said.

70.8.8.9.text: Eat something before you go back out. I mean that. I'm still a nurse.

70.8.9.1.text: Old. Works. That's all gear needs to be.

70.8.9.3.text: People come up asking about Aili's brother maybe once a year. I send them back down the road. You can go next door and buy bait. That's allowed.

70.8.9.4.text: Aili runs the motel and the bait counter next door. She'll give you coffee. She won't give you anything else. Don't push. I'll know.
70.8.9.4.note: asked where to ask, Ring nothing: it's next door

70.8.9.5.text: Liisa's my best summer kid. Don't get her in anything.

70.8.9.6.text: Gord's boat's at the dock. Atikokan. He brings bread and takes back gossip. Fair trade.

70.8.9.7.text: There's a fella on the Crane dock in shoes that never touched a boat. I don't like him. I don't like most people. I really don't like him.

70.8.9.8.text: Aili put out two cups this morning. One for you, she said. Go before it's cold.
70.8.9.8.note: Only if the player kept Walt out of print

70.8.9.9.text: She's not coming to the counter today. Or tomorrow. Buy your bait from me.

70.8.9.10.text: Bait's here. Aili's closed for you.

70.8.10.1.text: The post office taught me not to ask what's in a package. It works on packs too.

70.8.10.2.text: He worked this counter before me. I knew him from the post office. He'd come in for the mail and leave without it half the time, talking walleye with whoever was in line.

70.8.10.3.text: His handwriting was the kind you could read from across the room. Capital letters on the bait receipts. Nobody does that.

70.8.10.4.text: That's his hand. I sorted his mail for seven years. You don't forget a hand.

70.8.10.5.text: There's a woman in the bunkhouse says she's here to fish. Eleven days and one perch. I don't ask. Post office.

70.8.10.6.text: A man from the company asked if you'd been through. I said I don't keep track of customers. Which is a lie. I keep track of everything.

70.8.10.7.text: The woman from the bunkhouse sent me a postcard. From Duluth. 'Thanks for not asking.' Best mail I've had in years.

70.8.10.8.note: There isn't any. She means: nothing.

70.8.11.1.text: Canvas, brass grommets, leather. Thirty-eight pounds dry, I'd estimate. Considerably more wet.

70.8.11.2.text: No. I measured water, not people. I do know the lake he was found on. Birch. Mean depth about twenty feet. Not that it helps you.

70.8.11.3.text: Background station means upstream of anybody. Before anything's been touched. If a station's downstream of a pad, it's not background. That's not an opinion. That's what the word means.

70.8.11.4.text: The old filings are public. Anybody can ask the state. Nobody does. It's very boring reading, which is the point of it.

70.8.11.5.text: Nobody. I'm a long way up a forest road. I'm hard to ask.

70.8.11.6.text: They'll redo the baseline now. Properly. I'd like to see their numbers. I'd like to see anyone's numbers, honestly.

70.8.11.7.text: They'll build on the old baseline, then. Well. The water will say what it says. It always does, eventually.

70.8.12.1.text: That's an Ely pack, dear. We use lighter ones on the Trail. Take two lefse, you'll need them.

70.8.12.2.text: An Ely guide? On the Trail we don't keep track of Ely. They keep track of us, I think.

70.8.12.3.text: The one who drowned on the border? We heard. We hear everything eventually, a week late.

70.8.12.4.text: A young man from the mining company came all the way up the Trail with a hat for my husband. My husband wears it to bed. I'm not joking.

70.8.12.5.text: My husband read it and said, 'Well, that's those men, not the mine.' And I said yes. And we agreed about something for the first time since 2016.

70.8.12.6.text: Lefse's on the counter, dear. Help yourself.
70.8.12.6.note: Warm. She never knew Walt. This ending costs nothing here, and that is its own small point.

70.8.13.1.text: Somebody's. Mine's older. Mine's in the shed.

70.8.13.2.text: Knew him to nod at. He paddled the river once a year, slow. Looked at the old landings like they owed him rent.

70.8.13.3.text: The river? Lot of people think it's somebody's spot. It's rocks. It's everybody's rocks.

70.8.13.4.text: August of '19. Two fellas, green Kevlar, a week on the river. Bought gas. No bait. No rods. Asked me which way the old guide went. I said what old guide. I notice what people don't buy.
70.8.13.4.note: or the Isabella camp found, Corroborates the watchers' camp. Not a key, never names anyone.

70.8.13.5.text: Company kid with a card. I'm on his side and I still didn't like him asking.

70.8.13.6.text: Faked the water. Hm. I'm still for the mine. I'm against liars. I've been against liars longer.

70.8.13.7.note: He goes back to the tumpline.

70.8.14.1.text: Oh, I want to paint it. Can I paint it? It's so brown. I love brown.

70.8.14.2.text: Before me! I came up in 2020. I heard about him, though. Everybody up here has a story about somebody who drowned. Then they change the subject to the weather.

70.8.14.3.text: There's a white rock on a stump at the Little John landing. I painted it. Well, the landing. The rock's in it. It looked like somebody put it there on purpose.
70.8.14.3.note: A confirmation of the player's own pattern, never the first stone they hear of

70.8.14.4.text: Nobody comes up the Arrowhead Trail! Except you. And the propane truck.

70.8.14.5.text: I read the paper and then I painted the lake. It's the same lake. It just felt different.

70.8.14.6.text: Somebody said you got money. Do you want a painting? Kidding. Kind of.

70.9.1.text: Old guide used to camp here alone, they say. Always left a rock on the stump.
70.9.1.note: A starred site, stone in sight

70.9.2.text: This was somebody's favourite lake. Everybody's got one. Some people have twelve.
70.9.2.note: A nickname lake, an old local

70.9.3.text: This was a railroad. They hauled pine out on it. You can still find spikes.

70.9.4.text: There was a lodge here once. My grandma waitressed in one like it. The rhubarb's still coming up.

70.9.5.text: The drill crews used to land there. Seventies. You can still see the crib under the water on a calm day.
70.9.5.note: Bald Eagle's west shore, old local

70.9.6.text: Somebody dug a hole up on that hill a few years back. Big one. Didn't find anything, I guess. They left a shovel.
70.9.6.note: Pietro's north-east hill, a party, The wrong hill, public from the water
